name: Pirojpur
tagline: Asia's largest guava belt — floating markets where boats trade by the kilo, a two-kilometre boat haat on the Kuriana canal, and the village where modernist poet Ahsan Habib was born.

guide.bestTime: July to September — the guava harvest and full monsoon water, when the floating markets and Noukar Haat run at full volume. October–February for the boatyards and mosques.
guide.gettingThere: By overnight launch from Dhaka Sadarghat (~10 hr to Hularhat / Pirojpur), or by road via Barisal (~50 km, ~1.5 hr). The guava orchards and floating markets cluster in Nesarabad (Swarupkathi) on the northern edge; Mathbaria and Indurkani sit closer to the Sundarbans.
guide.difficulty: Easy — most floating-market and orchard trips are short boat rides; the Bhandaria mosques and zamindari ruins are quick CNG hops.

mustVisit.name: Atghar Kuriana Floating Guava Market
mustVisit.description: A weekday floating wholesale market on the Sondha canal where small boats pile high with green and amber guavas — growers row out at dawn, traders moor their bigger boats mid-stream, and the kilo-rates are shouted across the water until early afternoon.
mustVisit.history: The Nesarabad orchards form one corner of a 31,000-acre guava belt across Pirojpur, Jhalokati and Barisal — the largest in Asia. The Atghar Kuriana market is the Pirojpur half of the trade; the Bhimruli market in Jhalokati is the sister site one canal across.

practical.hours: Roughly 9 am – 1 pm, daily during the season
practical.entryFee: Boat hire only (negotiate at Kuriana ghat)

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 18 km north of Pirojpur town in Atghar Kuriana, Nesarabad (Swarupkathi) Upazila
howToReach.transport: CNG to Kuriana ghat, then small wooden boat into the canal

mustVisit.bestTime: July to September; August is the peak
tips: Go on a weekday — Friday morning is taken over by the boat haat further upstream
Buy directly from a grower's boat — it is cheaper, fresher and the right etiquette
Pair with Atghar–Kuriana orchard walk on dry land

mustVisit.name: Kuriana Boat Market (Noukar Haat)
mustVisit.description: A two-kilometre weekly boat market on the Kuriana canal — every Friday in the rains, hundreds of newly-built wooden 'panshi' country boats line the bank for sale, builders standing at their bows, the air heavy with mangosteen tar.
mustVisit.history: Held on the Kuriana canal between Banaripara (Barisal) and Swarupkathi (Pirojpur), the Noukar Haat is the country's biggest boat-selling market. Boats are built in the surrounding villages of Chami, Boitha Kata, Dubi and Kathali — coated in tar and mangosteen tannin to make them watertight.

practical.hours: Friday mornings during the monsoon (roughly Ashar–Ashwin)
practical.entryFee: Free; small boat hire to row through the haat

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 20 km north of Pirojpur on the Kuriana canal, between Banaripara and Swarupkathi
howToReach.transport: CNG to Kuriana, hire a small boat at the haat

tips: Get there by mid-morning — the haat thins out after midday
Watch a builder at work in one of the village yards — Boitha Kata is the easiest to reach
Don't expect a tourist-grade arrangement; this is a working market

mustVisit.name: Bibichini Shahi Mosque (Bhandaria)
mustVisit.description: A 17th-century single-domed brick mosque at Sarengkati in Bhandaria — squat walls, octagonal corner turrets and a single dome set on an octagonal drum. One of the southwestern coast's older surviving Mughal-era mosques.
mustVisit.history: Built around 1660–80 by Bibi Chini, daughter of Mughal Emperor Shah Shuja, on a fief said to have been granted to a local pir by Emperor Shah Jahan. Stands at Sarengkati village in Bhandaria Upazila, protected as an archaeological monument.

practical.hours: Daylight hours; mosque opens around prayer times

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 30 km south of Pirojpur town in Sarengkati, Bhandaria Upazila
howToReach.transport: Bus / CNG to Bhandaria, then rickshaw to Sarengkati

mustVisit.bestTime: Late afternoon for the brickwork light
tips: Cover head if female; remove shoes before entering
Combine with Mathbaria coastal villages on the same day

mustVisit.name: Rayerkati Zamindarbari & Shiva Mandir
mustVisit.description: The crumbling brick palace and adjoining Shiva temple of the Rayerkati zamindar family — banyan-tangled walls, terracotta panels and a still-active Shiva mandir in the inner courtyard.
mustVisit.history: Seat of the Rayerkati zamindars, one of the old Hindu landed families of greater Bakerganj, dating from the 18th–19th centuries. The temple complex remains in worship; parts of the rajbari are restored.

practical.entryFee: Free; small donation at the mandir

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 10 km east of Pirojpur town in Rayerkati, Pirojpur Sadar

mustVisit.bestTime: Cool months; Shiva Chaturdashi for the festival
tips: Mind your step — parts of the rajbari are unstable
Photograph the terracotta panels; do not climb the walls

mustVisit.name: Ahsan Habib's Shankarpasha
mustVisit.description: The home village of the modernist poet Ahsan Habib — a quiet Sadar-upazila settlement with a small memorial library at the family bari. A pilgrimage for anyone who has read 'Megh Bole Chaitre Jabo.'
mustVisit.history: Ahsan Habib (1917–1985), one of the great modernist voices of Bengali poetry, was born here on 2 February 1917. He spent his working life in Dhaka and Kolkata; his ancestral house in Shankarpasha holds his books, photographs and personal letters.

practical.hours: Daylight; ask at the family home / local school

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 5 km from Pirojpur town in Shankarpasha village, Pirojpur Sadar

mustVisit.bestTime: Cool months; 2 February (his birthday) for a small annual gathering
tips: Bring a copy of his poems — locals appreciate the reverence
The memorial is informal — ask at the village if the bari is open

mustVisit.name: Nesarabad Backwaters & Guava Orchards
mustVisit.description: The canal-and-orchard country of Nesarabad — a maze of narrow waterways threading 31,000 acres of guava trees. Hire a wooden boat in monsoon and drift between orchards where families pluck fruit from canoes pulled alongside.
mustVisit.history: The Pirojpur-Jhalokati-Barisal guava belt has been worked for over a century — the trees thrive on the silted canal banks and harvested fruit goes straight onto boats for the floating markets. About 20,000 farming families across 26 villages live off the trade.

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 18–22 km north of Pirojpur town; ghats at Kuriana, Atghar and Adamkathi
howToReach.transport: CNG to a ghat, then small wooden boat

mustVisit.bestTime: July to September — full water and ripe guava
tips: Negotiate hourly boat hire at the ghat before stepping in
Buy guava off the harvester boats — fresh, sweet, almost free
Carry rain protection — afternoon showers are routine

specialties.name: Swarupkathi Guava (Peyara)
specialties.description: Crisp, fragrant white-flesh guava — the variety the Nesarabad orchards are built on. Eaten raw with salt and chilli straight off the boat in season.
specialties.venue: Atghar Kuriana floating market & orchard ghats (Jul–Sep)

specialties.name: Kuriana Panshi Boat
specialties.description: Hand-built wooden country boats from Chami, Boitha Kata, Dubi and Kathali villages — sealed with tar and mangosteen tannin, sold at the weekly Friday boat haat.
specialties.venue: Kuriana boat haat & village boatyards (monsoon Fridays)

specialties.name: Coconut & Date-Palm Gur
specialties.description: Bhandaria and Mathbaria are coconut country; the date-palm villages produce nalen gur and patali in the cold months — winter sweet shops live off both.

bucketlist.title: Buy guava off a grower's boat at Atghar Kuriana
bucketlist.detail: A weekday wholesale market on the Sondha canal — small boats pile high with green and amber fruit, kilo-rates shouted across the water, the air sweet with ripe guava.

bucketlist.title: Row through the Kuriana Noukar Haat
bucketlist.detail: Two kilometres of newly-built wooden panshi boats lining the Kuriana canal every Friday in the rains — Bangladesh's biggest boat market, with builders standing at their bows.

bucketlist.title: Find Bibichini Shahi Mosque
bucketlist.detail: A 17th-century single-domed Mughal mosque at Sarengkati in Bhandaria, said to be built by Bibi Chini, a daughter of Emperor Shah Shuja.

bucketlist.title: Walk Rayerkati Zamindarbari at sunset
bucketlist.detail: Crumbling brick rajbari and a still-active Shiva mandir of the Rayerkati zamindars — banyan-tangled walls, terracotta panels and the quietest corner of Pirojpur Sadar.

bucketlist.title: Visit Ahsan Habib's Shankarpasha
bucketlist.detail: The village where the modernist poet Ahsan Habib (Megh Bole Chaitre Jabo) was born in 1917 — a small memorial at the family bari, quiet and unceremonious.

bucketlist.title: Drift through a Nesarabad guava orchard by boat
bucketlist.detail: Narrow canals threading 31,000 acres of guava trees — families pluck fruit from canoes pulled alongside; you drift, eat, and don't pay much.

bucketlist.title: Watch a panshi being built at Boitha Kata
bucketlist.detail: The village yards along the Kuriana canal where each Friday's boats are made — adze and gum and mangosteen tar, hands black with pitch.

bucketlist.title: Take the Hularhat–Sadarghat overnight launch
bucketlist.detail: The classic 10-hour Pirojpur-to-Dhaka launch journey — boarding at dusk at Hularhat, sleeping through the rivers, docking at dawn at Sadarghat.

bucketlist.title: Drive to the Sundarbans edge at Mathbaria
bucketlist.detail: The southern tip of Pirojpur, where coastal villages and shrimp farms back into the Sundarbans buffer — a quieter alternative to Mongla.

bucketlist.title: Buy date-palm gur in Bhandaria
bucketlist.detail: Bhandaria's winter date-palm villages produce some of the country's best nalen gur and patali — pour it on pitha at a roadside stall.

foods.name: Swarupkathi Peyara (Guava)
foods.description: Crisp, fragrant white-flesh guava — the variety the whole Nesarabad guava belt is built on. Eaten raw with salt and chilli straight off the boat.
foods.whereToFind: Atghar Kuriana floating market & orchard ghats (Jul–Sep)

foods.name: Floating-Market Daab (Green Coconut)
foods.description: Cold green coconut from char gardens, hawked from boats — the antidote to a humid orchard afternoon.

foods.name: Nalen Gur & Patali (Date-Palm Jaggery)
foods.description: Bhandaria's winter date-palm villages turn out some of the country's best raw and set jaggery — eaten on pitha or stirred into milk.
foods.whereToFind: Bhandaria and Mathbaria town sweet shops (Dec–Feb)

foods.name: Pirojpur Hilsa (Sandha River)
foods.description: Hilsa from the Sandha and Kacha rivers — slightly leaner than Bhola's Meghna fish, but pulled fresh into Hularhat ghat each morning in season.

famousPeople.name: Ahsan Habib
famousPeople.knownFor: Modernist Bengali poet, novelist and editor — one of the central voices of post-1947 Bangla poetry. Books include Ratri Shesh (1947), Sara Dupur (1964) and Megh Bole Chaitre Jabo (1976). Born 2 February 1917 in Shankarpasha village of Pirojpur Sadar; awarded the Bangla Academy Literary Award (1961) and Ekushey Padak (1978).

didYouKnow: The Nesarabad–Jhalokati–Barisal belt holds Asia's largest contiguous guava orchard — about 31,000 acres across 26 villages, with some 20,000 families depending on the trade.
Pirojpur's Atghar Kuriana floating market and the Bhimruli market across the canal in Jhalokati form one of the few year-round floating wholesale fruit markets in the world.
The weekly Kuriana Noukar Haat — held Fridays through the monsoon on a 2-km stretch of the Kuriana canal — is Bangladesh's biggest boat-selling market.
Bibichini Shahi Mosque in Bhandaria was built around 1660–80 by Bibi Chini, daughter of Mughal Emperor Shah Shuja, on a fief granted to a local pir.
Modernist poet Ahsan Habib — author of 'Megh Bole Chaitre Jabo' and recipient of the 1978 Ekushey Padak — was born in 1917 in Shankarpasha village of Pirojpur Sadar.
Kuriana's village boat-builders coat their newly-finished panshi boats with tar and the tannin of mangosteen bark to seal them against the water.
